newsitem.title: INDIA: Chidambaram to study Indian left's budget demands.
newsitem.headline: Chidambaram to study Indian left's budget demands.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Tuesday told leaders of four powerful left-wing allies that he would examine their demands for changes to his pathbreaking 1997/98 budget.
"I have heard their views. Let us see how much we can accommodate, how many suggestions are acceptable. We will examine it," Chidambaram told Reuters after the meeting.
"I told them I will do my best to consider their points of view."
Chidambaram also met a delegation of the main opposition, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), whose leaders said the minister was positive in his approach.
The meetings were scheduled ahead of a vote to iron out hitches in the passage of the budget and avoid rancour, particularly with leftist allies.

The lower house of parliament was expected to begin discussing the Finance Bill, which contains tax and tariff proposals, on Wednesday. Voting on the package, which has won praise from domestic and foreign investors, is expected by the end of the week.
"I will move the Finance Bill tomorrow," Chidambaram said.
The lower house on Tuesday approved spending plans for federal ministries forming part of the budget package.

The leaders of the four leftist parties, a powerful bloc within Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition, said they objected to budget proposals on insurance, duties and taxes on personal income and stock dividends.
"I see no major changes in the finance minister's position on major issues," said Biplab Dasgupta, a leader of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPM), after the meeting.
"On individual items like small industries and some import items he is interested to look into the issues," he said.
Asked whether left-wing parties would move amendments to the budget in parliament if Chidambaram did not accept their suggestions, Dasgupta said: "That we have not decided."
The four parties have 52 deputies in the 542-seat lower house of parliament. The United Front controls 178 seats.

Chidambaram has proposed reducing the tax rate on annual personal incomes of more than 150,000 rupees ($4,200) to 30 percent from 40 percent. He has also proposed lowering tax rates for incomes below that level.
Under Chidambaram's proposals, shareholders would be exempted from a tax on dividends. The corporate tax rate would be cut to 35 percent from an effective rate of 43 percent.
BJP leader Satish Aggarwal told reporters after his party's meeting with Chidambaram that it had opposed a proposal in the Finance Bill to levy a 10 percent tax on dividends distributed by companies.
The BJP had already given notice it would move around 50 amendments to the Finance Bill, he said.
"The finance minister's response was very positive. He was very cordial," Aggarwal said.
He said the BJP was not opposed to key cuts in individual and corporate tax proposed by Chidambaram. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
